paragraphs.text: The Mashgiach opens with the parsha of 'kedoshim tihyu', which Rashi says was said to the whole assembly, and notes that the verse names both 'Hashem' and 'Elokeichem'. Chanoch shut himself away, learned and davened until his flesh became fire and he became an angel, but he neglected his generation. Avraham never became an angel, because he dealt with Arabs and idolaters, yet he laid the foundation of a nation that serves Hashem.

Chanoch is the aspect of 'Hashem', closeness above; Avraham is 'Elokeichem', going down to the lowest of creation. Holiness, the Mashgiach says, must not contradict a bond with people. He then brings the Chasam Sofer that Nadav and Avihu were reincarnated in Pinchas, who is Eliyahu: they brought fire of their own, and their repair came when Eliyahu at Mount Carmel waited for fire from heaven.

The days of Sefirah, as the prayer said after counting shows, are days of tikkun and teshuvah, to be cleansed and come pure to Matan Torah. There are three such seasons: Sefirah, Shovavim and Elul-Tishrei, and the Mashgiach asks how they differ. He begins with Nissan, 'the head of the months', and brings the Maharal that a beginning lasts for its first quarter, which is why the light of creation still shone at Chanukah.

blocks.heading: Nissan's growth and the burned se'ir

paragraphs.text: By the same measure, the beginning of Nissan extends over Nissan, Iyar and Sivan, a season of birth and growth: Klal Yisroel was born at the Exodus, and in nature the trees blossom and later bear fruit.

The Mashgiach then asks about the verse in Shemini: the first se'ir of Rosh Chodesh, offered on the day the Mishkan was set up, was burned and not eaten. Since a beginning is a sign, what kind of sign is this for all generations? He also asks how Nadav and Avihu, whom Moshe called greater than himself, could rule a halacha before their teacher and, as the Midrash says, enter after drinking wine.

blocks.heading: Tishrei and Nissan: din and chesed

paragraphs.text: To answer, the Mashgiach brings the dispute of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua whether the world was created in Tishrei or in Nissan, and Tosafos that both are true. Nissan, when trees blossom, is the birth of creation; Tishrei, the time of gathering, is its bar mitzvah, when everything stands complete.

Tishrei is a beginning of din, with fasting and Selichos; Nissan is a beginning of chesed, and Rabbi Pinchas of Koretz says the judgment of Sefirah is greater than the Ten Days of Teshuvah, only it comes with chesed. Each Tanna follows his approach: Rabbi Eliezer, the strict one, sees creation in din, and Rabbi Yehoshua of Beis Hillel in chesed. For Rabbi Eliezer the beginning is hinted at Bereishis, though the world truly began from its middle, Eretz Yisroel.

For Rabbi Yehoshua the beginning is hinted in the middle of the Torah. Just as Bereishis hints at the six hundred thousand letters and souls, the Masorah marks the middle of the Torah at 'darosh darash', said of the se'ir of the chatas, and the Mashgiach reads 'se'ir' as hinting to the six hundred thousand explanations of the Torah. He then explains, with Rashi, that the se'ir of Rosh Chodesh atones for the lessening of the moon, which is Klal Yisroel in galus.

blocks.heading: The day the Mishkan was set up

paragraphs.text: Rosh Chodesh Nissan is the head of all heads, and the first one, the day the Mishkan was set up, was, as the Gemara in Megillah says, a joy like the day of creation. It was a sample of the world repaired, of the days of Moshiach, which will return permanently when Moshiach comes.

This answers the question. The se'ir is eaten as atonement for the lessening of the moon, but on that day Klal Yisroel was whole and the moon shone in full. No atonement was needed, so not eating it was the finest sign for all generations. That is why it is hinted at the very middle of the Torah.

blocks.heading: Nadav and Avihu sensed the days of Moshiach

paragraphs.text: Nadav and Avihu did not simply die; as the Zohar reads 'Pinchas ben Elazar ben Aharon', they entered Pinchas, who is Eliyahu, the herald of the redemption. So the Torah says 'after the death' of Aharon's sons: they are already beyond death, at the level where death will be swallowed up forever.

When Moshiach comes, the Mashgiach says, there will be no rebbe and talmid; as Yirmiyahu says, no one will need to teach another, for the Torah will be written on the heart. On the day of the Mishkan the people felt a taste of this, and Nadav and Avihu, more sensitive than anyone, felt it so strongly that they lost themselves. They ruled before their teacher and entered after drinking wine, which shows their greatness, not their smallness.

The Gemara in Berachos asks why one does not bentch after wine, though it satisfies and 'gladdens the heart', and answers that people do not make it a fixed meal. If someone does, it says, Eliyahu will decide. The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that wine makes a man first like a sheep, then a lion, a monkey and a pig, and the Gemara that wine's end is blood.

Yayin is seventy: twenty-six, Hashem's Name, plus forty-four, dam. A little wine for serving Hashem with joy holds the Name; too much leaves only blood. Kiddush therefore begins 'Yom hashishi vayechulu', whose initials form the Name, as the Chasam Sofer notes. One born under Ma'adim, says the Gemara in Shabbos, is connected with blood, and Eliyahu is the holy side of that mazal. When he comes, wine will harm no more; Nadav and Avihu felt that time and entered after drinking.

From the first day of Pesach to Shavuos there are fifty-one days, just as from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Shemini Atzeres, and the Mashgiach hints this in the two 'na' of 'Ana Hashem' in Hallel. The thirtieth day of Elul is Rosh Hashanah; the thirtieth of Sefirah is Pesach Sheni, a day of repair for those who could not bring the Pesach.

According to the Gemara, the men impure at the first Pesach were Mishael and Eltzafan, who became impure from Nadav and Avihu. Through that soul, which is beyond death, they merited the parsha of Pesach Sheni and showed that even impurity of death can be repaired.

blocks.heading: The middos are the root of sin

paragraphs.text: Now the Mashgiach reaches his main point. Sefirah is for repairing the middos, chesed, gevurah, tiferes, netzach and hod, so that each is used for good. Rabbi Chaim Vital writes in Shaarei Kedushah that the middos are the root of all the mitzvos, and a bad midda is much worse than a sin, as the Be'er Mayim Chaim explains on Tazria: one who sins does teshuvah on the sin, but the root is the midda.

Lashon hara is the worst sin, but it is only the fruit; its root is arrogance, the need to feel big by making another small. Machlokes grows from the need to win: Yeravam ben Nevat, the greatest scholar of his generation, could not bear to stand while Rechavam sat in the Beis HaMikdash, so he set up the golden calves. Eating something doubtful grows from desire.

This is why, the Mashgiach says, many people do teshuvah and then fall into the same sin: they repented on the sin and not on the midda. Had they repaired the root, they would not have come to the sin.

The Mashgiach goes through the middos. Chesed: give tzedakah, do a favor, learn with someone, even at the cost of one's own time. Gevurah: be strong against the yetzer hara, even in permitted foods. Tiferes: know that one is a great soul, so that every mitzvah, even counting the Omer, is enormous. Netzach: fight for Yiddishkeit, not to show another up. Hod: bow down and sing praise to Hashem.

This answers the opening question. Nissan, when roots sprout, is the time to repair the root, the middos. Tishrei, the harvest, is for teshuvah on deeds. Shovavim is a laundry season: as Rabbeinu Yonah writes, a stain remains even after teshuvah, and then it is removed. Through their self-sacrifice, Nadav and Avihu also merited for Aharon entry into the Kodesh HaKodashim, 'with this he shall come'.

blocks.heading: The Rambam's Sefer Kedushah in Sefirah

paragraphs.text: Acharei-Kedoshim falls in the middle of Sefirah, the week of netzach, the axis around which Sefirah turns; Acharei speaks of taharah and Kedoshim of kedushah. The Mashgiach shows that almost all of the Rambam's Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah is in the Sefirah parshiyos: forbidden foods and impurities in Shemini, blood in Acharei, forbidden relations in Acharei and Kedoshim, and impurity of the dead in Emor.

Even the few exceptions connect: the gid hanasheh, the ox that is stoned and wine of idolaters. Rabbeinu Bachya says the stoned ox is forbidden because the angel of death rode on it, the same source as impurity of death.

The Ramban explains that 'kedoshim tihyu' means to separate oneself even in permitted things. Without it, one could eat and drink without limit and be a glutton within the Torah's permission; so the Torah commands to sanctify oneself in what is permitted. This, the Mashgiach says, is the repair of middos rather than deeds.

Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim 231 states it as halacha, not mussar: all one's eating, drinking and speech should be for serving Hashem. The Mashgiach adds that ours is a very weak generation, unable to demand great things of itself.

Yet the parsha was said to the whole congregation, so 'kedoshim tihyu' is for everyone, each by his measure, with sense. A small offering is also precious to Hashem. One need not always take the ice cream or the piece of chocolate; one should eat enough to be content and serve Hashem with joy. As the Bnei Yissaschar says, the Torah cannot set the amount; each must measure himself and, hardest of all, not fool himself.

The Mashgiach closes by urging the listeners to use the remaining weeks of Sefirah: look out the window at the trees blossoming and the grass growing each day, and do not lag behind nature. The middos and the soul should grow better each day until Matan Torah.
